title: Zeeman Effect
short_intro: The Zeeman effect is the splitting of a spectral line into several components in the presence of a static magnetic field. It arises from the interaction of the magnetic moment associated with the angular momentum of the atomic electrons with the external magnetic field.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Qualitative understanding of normal Zeeman effect, splitting of spectral lines, role of weak magnetic fields, and selection rules (delta m = 0, +/- 1).
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Quantitative derivation of Zeeman shift, Normal vs. Anomalous Zeeman effect, Lande g-factor, Paschen-Back effect, and Stark effect comparison.

prerequisites: Electron spin and orbital angular momentum

concept_notes.heading: Phenomenology of the Zeeman Effect
bullets: When a light source emitting a line spectrum is placed in a uniform magnetic field, individual spectral lines split into multiple equidistant components.
Discovered by Pieter Zeeman in 1896, it provided direct evidence for the spatial quantization of angular momentum in atoms.
The magnitude of the frequency shift is proportional to the magnetic field strength and independent of the initial unperturbed frequency to a first approximation.

concept_notes.heading: Normal Zeeman Effect
bullets: Observed in singlet spectral lines (total spin S = 0, so total angular momentum J = L).
A single spectral line splits into precisely three components: an unshifted central pi component (delta m = 0) and two symmetrically shifted sigma components (delta m = +/- 1).
It is adequately explained by classical electron theory combined with quantum mechanical spatial quantization.

concept_notes.heading: Anomalous Zeeman Effect
bullets: Observed in doublet, triplet, or higher multiplet lines where electron spin is non-zero (S != 0).
The spectral line splits into more than three components (often 4, 6, or more).
Requires the introduction of the Lande g-factor to account for the differing contributions of orbital and spin angular momenta to the total magnetic moment.

concept_notes.heading: Lande g-Factor and Magnetic Moment
bullets: The magnetic moment of an electron is not simply proportional to its total angular momentum J due to the anomalous gyromagnetic ratio for spin (g_s approx 2).
The Lande g-factor is given by g = 1 + \frac{J(J+1) + S(S+1) - L(L+1)}{2J(J+1)}.
It determines the precise energy level splitting in a weak magnetic field for the anomalous Zeeman effect.

derivations.title: Normal Zeeman Shift Derivation
derivations.conditions: Weak magnetic field, singlet states (S=0, J=L)
steps: Consider an electron orbiting a nucleus with orbital angular momentum L. The circulating charge constitutes a current loop with magnetic dipole moment mu_L = - \frac{e}{2m} L.
In the presence of an external magnetic field B directed along the z-axis, the potential energy of interaction is Delta E = - \mu_L \cdot B = - \mu_{Lz} B_z.
Using the spatial quantization condition for the z-component of orbital angular momentum, L_z = m_l \hbar, we get Delta E = \frac{e \hbar B}{2m} m_l.
Expressed in terms of angular frequency shift, Delta \omega = \frac{eB}{2m} = \omega_L, where \omega_L is the Larmor frequency.
derivations.result: Delta E = m_l \mu_B B, where \mu_B is the Bohr magneton.

derivations.title: Anomalous Zeeman Energy Splitting
derivations.conditions: Weak magnetic field, arbitrary L, S, and J
steps: The total magnetic moment operator is the sum of orbital and spin contributions: \mu = \mu_B (L + 2S) / \hbar.
Projecting this magnetic moment onto the total angular momentum vector J, the effective magnetic moment is \mu_{eff} = -g \frac{e}{2m} J.
The energy shift in a weak magnetic field B is given by the expectation value Delta E = - \langle \mu \cdot B \rangle.
Substituting the Lande g-factor, the energy shift becomes Delta E = m_j g \mu_B B, where m_j takes values from -j to +j.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Normal Zeeman Effect Splitting Diagram
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Energy levels splitting into 3 sub-levels for m_l = -1, 0, 1 with vertical transitions governed by delta m = 0, +/- 1.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows the origin of the unshifted pi line and the two symmetrically shifted sigma lines.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in TGT/PGT to identify the number of components in normal Zeeman splitting.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Lummer-Gehrcke Plate / Fabry-Perot Etalon Setup
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: An electromagnet with pole pieces containing a discharge tube, followed by lenses and a high-resolution interferometer (Fabry-Perot etalon) projecting rings on a screen.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: High-resolution optical setup required because the wavelength shifts in Zeeman effect are extremely small.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual questions on experimental apparatus used to observe fine splitting.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Polarization of Zeeman Components
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: View parallel to B field showing only sigma components (circularly polarized); view perpendicular to B field showing pi component (plane polarized parallel to B) and sigma components (plane polarized perpendicular to B).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the vector nature of radiation emitted by precessing atomic dipoles.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Direct factual questions in PGT physics regarding polarization states of pi and sigma lines.

solved_numericals.question: A spectral line of wavelength 5890 Angstrom is subjected to a magnetic field of 1 Tesla. Calculate the separation between the Zeeman components assuming normal Zeeman effect. Take e/m = 1.76 x 10^11 C/kg and c = 3 x 10^8 m/s.
solution_steps: Formula: Delta lambda = (e * lambda^2 * B) / (4 * pi * m * c)
Convert wavelength to meters: lambda = 5890 x 10^-10 m
Result: Delta lambda = 1.62 x 10^-15 m = 0.0162 Angstrom

solved_numericals.question: For a 2P_3/2 to 2S_1/2 transition in an atom, compute the Lande g-factor for the 2P_3/2 state and determine the number of Zeeman components observed in a weak magnetic field.
solution_steps: Find maximum number of transitions using selection rules: m_j changes by 0, +/- 1. Upper level has 4 states (m_j = 3/2, 1/2, -1/2, -3/2), lower level has 2 states (m_j = 1/2, -1/2). Total allowed transitions give 6 components.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the magnetic field strength B required to produce a Zeeman splitting equal to the natural line width of a spectral line of wavelength 5000 Angstrom having a lifetime tau = 10^-8 seconds.
solution_steps: Natural line width in frequency: Delta nu = 1 / (2 * pi * tau) = 1 / (2 * 3.1416 * 10^-8) = 1.59 x 10^7 Hz
Normal Zeeman frequency shift: Delta nu = (e * B) / (4 * pi * m)
Equate frequency shift to line width: (e / 4 pi m) * B = 1.59 x 10^7

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumes the applied magnetic field is weak compared to the internal spin-orbit coupling magnetic field (Zeeman regime, not Paschen-Back regime).
Neglects nuclear spin effects (hyperfine structure is ignored).

common_misconceptions.wrong: All spectral lines split into exactly three components in a magnetic field.
common_misconceptions.correct: Only singlet lines (Normal Zeeman effect) split into three components; multi-electron atoms with spin show anomalous Zeeman effect with multiple components.
common_misconceptions.why: Electron spin introduces an additional magnetic moment contribution that alters the simple 3-level splitting pattern.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Zeeman effect requires an electric field.
common_misconceptions.correct: Zeeman effect is exclusively caused by a magnetic field, whereas the Stark effect is caused by an electric field.
common_misconceptions.why: Magnetic dipole interaction with B-field governs Zeeman splitting, not electric dipole interaction.

quick_revision: Normal Zeeman effect occurs for S=0 states and yields exactly 3 components (1 pi, 2 sigma).
Anomalous Zeeman effect occurs when S != 0 and is governed by the Lande g-factor.
Bohr magneton has the standard value mu_B = e hbar / 2m.
Selection rules for Zeeman transitions are Delta m_j = 0, +/- 1.
